title: Review: Periodic trends; Emission spectra and energy levels; IE evidence for sub-shells (period 3 dips); Orbitals and electron configuration
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Edexcel A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: AS03#t2 term and clue written for the game; AS04#t2 term and clue written for the game; AS03#t3 term and clue written for the game; AS03#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: AS03#N.3a, AS04#N.6a, AS06#N.4, PT02#N.14, AS03#N.9, AS04#N.9a, AS06#N.10, PT02#N.10, AS03#N.12, AS04#N.12a, AS06#N.6, PT02#N.4a. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Emission line spectrum
items.clue: Separate bright frequencies on a dark background, given out by excited atoms.

items.label: Hund's rule
items.clue: Electrons enter regions of equal energy singly, with parallel spins, before pairing.

items.label: Shell
items.clue: A main electron level, numbered n = 1, 2, 3, 4 outwards, holding at most 2n² electrons.

items.label: Photon
items.clue: Given out when an excited electron falls back; its energy equals the gap between levels.

questions.stem: When sodium compounds are heated in a flame, the flame turns yellow. Which process in the sodium atoms produces this yellow light?

options.text: Excited electrons fall to lower energy levels, emitting photons.
Electrons absorb energy and emit photons as they rise to higher levels.
Electrons escape from the atoms entirely, releasing energy as photons.
The hot atoms glow with the yellow colour that sodium atoms possess.

questions.explanation: Each fall emits a photon whose energy equals the gap between the levels; sodium's main gap gives yellow light.

questions.stem: Which full electron configuration of a ground-state atom is correct?

options.text: scandium: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 4p¹
cobalt: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁹
iron: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁶ 4s²
germanium: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹² 4s²

questions.explanation: 18 electrons to 3p⁶, then 4s², then six in 3d: 26 in all.

questions.stem: After the dip, the rise resumes: silicon's first ionisation energy is 787 kJ mol⁻¹, higher than aluminium's 578 kJ mol⁻¹. Why?

options.text: Silicon's electron is removed from 3s, which is lower in energy than aluminium's 3p.
Silicon's two 3p electrons are paired in one orbital, which holds them more firmly.
Silicon atoms are larger, so there is more space for the nucleus to attract its electrons.
Both electrons come from 3p, but silicon has one more proton and similar shielding.

questions.explanation: Same sub-shell, similar shielding, greater nuclear charge: the attraction is stronger, so more energy is needed.

questions.stem: An argon atom has seven more electrons than a sodium atom, yet argon's first ionisation energy is about three times sodium's. Which explains this?

options.text: Argon's outer shell is full, and a full shell is stable, so it does not want to lose an electron.
Argon has more electrons, so the extra electron–electron repulsion holds its outer electron in place.
Argon's outer electron is in a higher shell than sodium's, so it is held more tightly.
Argon has 18 protons to sodium's 11, and its outer electrons are in the same shell with similar shielding.

questions.stem: What is the maximum total number of electrons that the first three main energy levels of an atom (n = 1, 2 and 3) can hold?
An iron atom (Z = 26) has the condensed electron configuration [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². How is an Fe²⁺ ion formed from this atom?

options.text: Two of the six 3d electrons are removed from the atom.
One 4s electron and one 3d electron are each removed.
Two electrons are added to the 3d sub-shell of the atom.
Both of the 4s electrons are removed from the atom.

questions.explanation: Transition metal atoms lose 4s electrons before 3d: [Ar] 3d⁶, 24 electrons.

questions.stem: The first ionisation energies of beryllium and boron are 900 kJ mol⁻¹ and 801 kJ mol⁻¹. Which explanation of the lower value for boron is correct?

options.text: Boron's electron is removed from a 2p orbital that already holds another electron.
Boron atoms are larger than beryllium atoms, so the outer electron is further away.
Boron's electron is removed from 2p, which is higher in energy than beryllium's 2s.
Boron's nuclear charge is shared among more electrons, so each is held less strongly.

questions.stem: Fluorine is more electronegative than chlorine. Which explains this?

options.text: A fluorine atom has more protons than a chlorine atom, so it pulls harder on a shared pair.
Fluorine needs only one electron to fill its outer shell, so it attracts electrons strongly.
In fluorine the shared pair is closer to the nucleus and shielded by fewer inner electrons.
Fluorine releases more energy than chlorine when it gains an electron, so it is more electronegative.

questions.explanation: Fluorine's bonding electrons are in shell 2, shielded only by 1s². Chlorine's are in shell 3, shielded by 10 inner electrons. Shorter distance and less shielding outweigh chlorine's larger nuclear charge.

questions.stem: Lithium compounds give a crimson-red flame. Sodium compounds give a yellow-orange flame. Which statement explains the difference?

options.text: Lithium's electrons fall across a larger energy gap, because red light has the longer wavelength.
The flame is hotter around sodium, so the same transitions give out higher-energy light.
Sodium's excited electrons fall across a larger energy gap, so each photon has more energy.
Sodium's electrons give out yellow photons as the flame raises them to higher levels.

questions.stem: A ground-state phosphorus atom is [Ne] 3s² 3p³. Where are its three 3p electrons?

options.text: Together in one 3p orbital, which all three share.
On one circular orbit at a fixed distance from the nucleus.
Two paired in one 3p orbital, one in a second, the third left empty.
One in each of the three 3p orbitals, with parallel spins.

questions.explanation: Three equal-energy orbitals, three electrons: one each, spins parallel. Each electron is spread over its dumbbell-shaped region.

questions.stem: The first ionisation energies of phosphorus and sulfur are 1012 kJ mol⁻¹ and 1000 kJ mol⁻¹. Which explanation of the lower value for sulfur is correct?

options.text: Sulfur's outer electrons are shielded by more inner electrons than phosphorus's.
Sulfur's electron is removed from a sub-shell of higher energy than phosphorus's.
Sulfur loses an electron from a doubly occupied 3p orbital, where repulsion raises its energy.
Sulfur atoms are larger than phosphorus atoms, so their outer electron is further away.

questions.explanation: P has three unpaired 3p electrons; in S one 3p orbital holds a pair. Repulsion between them means slightly less energy is needed.

questions.stem: The ions Na⁺, F⁻, Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ all have the electron configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶. Which lists them in order of decreasing ionic radius?

options.text: O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺
O²⁻ = F⁻ = Na⁺ = Mg²⁺
Mg²⁺ > Na⁺ > F⁻ > O²⁻
Na⁺ > Mg²⁺ > O²⁻ > F⁻

questions.explanation: Same 10 electrons, so size depends on nuclear charge: 8, 9, 11 and 12 protons. More protons pull the same electrons closer, so radius decreases from O²⁻ to Mg²⁺.
